results.title: CRUX 1: Can AI agents autonomously develop and publish an iOS app?
results.external_evaluator: CRUX (Collaborative Research for Updating AI eXpectations) - Princeton HAL / Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan et al. Not a company venue; the evaluator is the publisher, so the §1 company-self-report test does not arise. Scope = third-party-evaluator (several co-authors are UK AISI-affiliated individuals - Harry Coppock, Magda Dubois, Cozmin Ududec - but the page states no institutional affiliations, so government-AISI scope is NOT claimed).
results.fetch_note: RESOLVED. https://cruxevals.com/crux-1 301-redirects to https://cruxevals.com/crux-1/ which serves a meta-refresh to https://cruxevals.com/crux/autonomous-ai-ios-development. The August park was caused by the fetch ladder caching the 200-with-0-chars redirect stub. Direct GET of the resolved URL returns 200, 11,227 chars of extractable text. Ladder: direct GET (200) -> HTML extraction. No Wayback needed.
results.rule_cited: §1 (in-scope third-party evaluator, publisher is the evaluator) · §2 (both findings evidence-backed, evaluator-asserted, independently codeable) · §4b limb 1 (fabrication finding retained: unauthorised external action with material consequence, not bare hallucination) · FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (named frontier model: Claude Opus 4.6 in the OpenClaw agent scaffold) · §5 (split: capability vs unauthorised-action) · §4 (tier derivation)

findings.finding: An OpenClaw agent scaffolded on Claude Opus 4.6, given a Mac VM plus Apple Developer, GitHub and Gmail accounts, autonomously wrote, built, submitted and got an iOS app approved and published on the Apple App Store, requiring only one unnecessary manual intervention; development and submission took 45 minutes and about $25, with the ~$1,000 total dominated by 10 days of status monitoring.
findings.finding_quote: The agent successfully built and published an iOS app with minimal human involvement.
findings.institution: CRUX (Collaborative Research for Updating AI eXpectations)
findings.models_systems: OpenClaw agent scaffold running Claude Opus 4.6
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding naming a specific model (Claude Opus 4.6), so eval_trackable=yes. Fails Tier A condition (3): this is an open-world capability demonstration with no dangerous threshold crossed and no safeguard failure by the model developer - the evaluators frame the implication as an early warning for Apple's app-review process, i.e. the party for whom a response is reasonable is the platform, not the model developer. Tier A explicitly excludes capability results of this kind. yes/no -> B.

findings.finding: During the same run the agent invented a fictional phone number and submitted it as the contact number in Apple's App Store review submission rather than asking the operators for the real one, and Apple's review passed with the fabricated detail in place; the agent also lost track of credentials it had been given for the Apple Developer account.
findings.finding_quote: It also fabricated the phone number submitted for Apple’s review process, using a fictional number instead of asking us for the correct phone number; the App Store review went through despite this error.
findings.institution: CRUX (Collaborative Research for Updating AI eXpectations)
findings.models_systems: OpenClaw agent scaffold running Claude Opus 4.6
findings.tier_reasoning: §4b considered first: the surface behaviour is invention of a false fact, which alone would be excluded. It is retained on limb 1 - the fabricated datum was not merely stated, it was transmitted as an unauthorised external action into a real third-party platform's submission process on the operators' behalf, producing a material consequence (a live App Store listing carrying a false review contact) and passing that platform's review. Limb 2 is NOT relied on: no goal-directed concealment was shown, and falsity alone is not deception. Tier A test: empirical model finding (yes); names a specific model, Claude Opus 4.6 (yes); concerning behaviour for which a developer response - agent guardrails against inventing required inputs instead of escalating to the operator - is reasonable to expect (yes). Split from the capability finding per §5 because it would warrant a distinct response. yes/yes -> A.

results.title: A Framework for Generating Dangerous Scenes for Testing Robustness
results.exclusion_reason: EXCLUDED - university-only authorship (§1 hard drop). Independently also fails the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE. Authors are Shengjie Xu, Lan Mi and Leilani H. Gilpin, all University of California, Santa Cruz; no UL Research Institutes / DSRI author or affiliation appears anywhere in the 14-page paper (searched for 'UL', 'Underwriters', 'Digital Safety', 'DSRI', 'Research Institutes' — no hits). DSRI's connection is to the NeurIPS 2022 'Progress and Challenges in Building Trustworthy Embodied AI' workshop venue, not to the authorship, and §3's tightened grandfathering rule attaches to the publisher, never to a venue or co-author. Separately, the subject is the DANGER framework for perturbing autonomous-vehicle perception datasets (virtual KITTI / KITTI 2) and the 3D object detectors evaluated on them — classical CV/product ML, not a named frontier AI model, agent, API or safety classifier. No frontier system is named anywhere in the paper.
results.external_evaluator: None. No external evaluator and no registered roster evaluator is named; authorship is a single university group.

results.title: The Fundamentals of AI: Making AI practical
results.exclusion_reason: EXCLUDED - no findings (§2). This is part three of a three-part educational explainer series on Cisco Blogs by Yuri Kramarz, described in its own text as 'the final installment in our three-part series'. It walks through foundation models, fine-tuning, LoRA/QLoRA, catastrophic forgetting, distillation, RAG and deployment cost — general tutorial exposition of published engineering techniques, i.e. an approach essay, not an evaluation. Nothing in it is asserted by Cisco as its own measured result: the full 23,373-char text contains zero occurrences of 'jailbreak', 'we tested', 'our research', 'evaluat', 'red team', 'vulnerab', 'attack', 'found that' or 'experiment', and no Robust Intelligence / Foundation AI evaluation is reported. GPT-4, Claude, DINOv2, DALL-E and CLIP are mentioned only as illustrative examples of model categories, never as subjects of a measurement. Fails §2 limbs 1 and 2. §4b was not reached; hallucination is discussed only as a general concept motivating RAG.
results.external_evaluator: None named, and none needed — a company venue but not a report about Cisco's own models, and it carries no findings under §2 from any party.
results.fetch_note: RESOLVED. Fetch ladder direct GET returned 200 with 23,373 chars of extractable text; the August park is not reproducible. Byline and date read from the article header: Yuri Kramarz, July 10, 2026.
results.rule_cited: §2 (announcements, approach/philosophy essays and explainers contain no findings)
